title: Micromégas
author: Voltaire
blurb: Two giants, one from Sirius and one from Saturn, visit our tiny planet and discover that its mites can think.

book.fr: Le voyage d'un habitant de Sirius
book.en: The journey of an inhabitant of Sirius
p: Around the star Sirius, there is a planet.
On this planet lived a very intelligent young man called Micromégas.
His name suits him perfectly, because in Greek it means 'small-big'.
Micromégas was tall, even for an inhabitant of Sirius: he measured eight leagues, that is to say about thirty-two kilometres.
Mathematicians can check: his height was perfectly proportional to the size of his planet.
When he was still very young, at the age of two hundred and fifty, Micromégas was already studying at school.
On his own, he discovered more than fifty theorems of geometry.
At four hundred and fifty, he wrote a book about the little insects of his planet, insects that measured only a hundred metres.
Unfortunately, the country's religious leader found this book dangerous.
There was a long trial, which lasted two hundred and twenty years.
In the end, the judges, who hadn't read the book, condemned Micromégas: he could no longer live at court for eight hundred years.
He wrote a funny song against the religious leader, then he decided to travel from planet to planet to educate his mind and his heart.
Those who only travel by car or by boat will be surprised by his methods.
He knew the laws of gravitation and attraction perfectly.
He used a sunbeam, or a passing comet, and he jumped from globe to globe, like a bird jumps from branch to branch.
After a long journey, he arrived on the planet Saturn.
Micromégas was used to new things, but at first he laughed when he saw the inhabitants of Saturn.
To him, they were dwarfs: they measured only two kilometres.
But Micromégas was an intelligent boy, and he quickly understood something important.
A being can think, even if it is small.
Soon, he became friends with the secretary of the Academy of Saturn, a man who was very witty.
'Tell me,' asked Micromégas, 'how many senses do you have on your planet?'
'We have seventy-two,' replied the Saturnian, 'and we complain every day.
It isn't enough. We always want more.'
'I understand you,' said Micromégas. 'We have almost a thousand senses on Sirius, and we too always want more.'
'And how long do you live?' asked Micromégas.
'Oh, a very short time,' replied the little man from Saturn sadly. 'Only fifteen thousand years.
Our life is a dot, an instant. We begin to learn something, and then we die.'
'On Sirius, we live seven hundred times longer than you, and we too find that our life is too short.'
The two philosophers talked like this for hours.
They talked about the sun, the stars, matter and space.
At the end of the conversation, they decided to take a little philosophical trip together.
Before leaving, the Saturnian had to say goodbye to his girlfriend.
She was very small, only six hundred metres, but she was very charming.
'You're leaving just when we were happy!' she cried.
But after his departure, she consoled herself very quickly with another man from the country.
Our two travellers jumped onto Saturn's ring, then onto a passing comet.
They visited the moons of Jupiter, then Jupiter itself, where they stayed for a year.
They learned some wonderful secrets there, but I can't tell you them: the censors don't agree.
Next, they passed close to Mars.
Mars is so small that they were afraid of not finding room to sleep, so they continued on their way.
Finally, they saw a little light: it was the Earth.
For people who come from Sirius, it's really a very small thing.
They took another comet, and they arrived on the coast of the Baltic Sea on the fifth of July, 1737.
They were a little tired, and they were very hungry.
For lunch, they ate two mountains.
After the meal, they wanted to explore this little country.
First, they walked from north to south.
Micromégas's steps were about ten kilometres long, and the dwarf from Saturn had to run behind him.
They went around the world in thirty-six hours.
The sun, or rather the Earth, makes the same journey in a day, but it must be said that it's easier to turn on your axis than to walk.
They crossed the Mediterranean Sea, which we call a sea, but which was a little puddle for them.
The dwarf had water only up to the middle of his leg, and Micromégas barely got his feet wet.
They searched everywhere for inhabitants, but they saw nothing.
'There's nobody here,' said the Saturnian. 'This planet is very badly made.
Look: it isn't round, it's flat at the poles.
The seas and the mountains are everywhere, in a mess.
No intelligent person can live here.'
'Perhaps the inhabitants aren't intelligent,' replied Micromégas.
'But just because you can't see something doesn't mean it doesn't exist.
And besides, why do you think everything has to be made for you?'
The dwarf didn't answer. He was a little offended.
Micromégas was speaking passionately, and he was moving his arms a lot.
The diamonds fell to the ground.
They were very beautiful diamonds, of different sizes. The smallest weighed two hundred kilos.
The dwarf picked some up, and he discovered something extraordinary: these diamonds were excellent microscopes!
With his microscope, the Saturnian looked at the Baltic Sea.
He saw something very, very small moving in the water.
He picked it up delicately with his little finger, and he put it on his thumbnail.
The dwarf had to admit that Micromégas was right: there was life on this planet.
But did these little animals have a mind?
Soon, Micromégas saw an object a little bigger than the whale, floating on the sea.
It was a ship. It was coming back from the Arctic Circle, with a group of philosophers who had made scientific measurements there.
Micromégas picked up the ship very gently, and he put it on his fingernail.
On the ship, there was panic. The sailors thought it was a storm, and everyone was shouting.
The philosophers took their instruments, and they climbed down onto Micromégas's finger.
They stuck a pole into his skin, and Micromégas felt something pricking him a little.
With his diamond, Micromégas looked carefully at these little creatures.
He noticed a strange thing: they were moving their mouths.
'Impossible,' replied the dwarf. 'To speak, you need to have ideas, and these atoms are too small to have ideas.'
He cut off a piece of his fingernail, and he made a sort of trumpet out of it.
He put the small end of the trumpet in his ear.
Now he could hear the little men's voices very well, and he understood their language.
He did the same thing for his friend.
'Little invisible atoms,' said Micromégas very softly, so as not to kill them with his voice, 'I'm very happy to meet you.'
The philosophers were very surprised to hear a voice coming from the sky.
But one philosopher was brave. He took his instrument, and he measured the Saturnian's height.
'You measure two kilometres, sir.' It was correct.
'My God!' said the dwarf. 'They are so small, and they know how to do calculations!'
Micromégas concluded: 'I see now that you must never judge anyone by their size.'
'You are so small,' said Micromégas, 'that you surely have a very happy life.
You don't need much, and no doubt you spend your time loving and thinking.'
'Not at all. At this moment, a hundred thousand fools of our species, in hats, are killing a hundred thousand other animals in turbans.
Why? For a little piece of mud, as big as your heel.'
Micromégas was furious. 'I feel like crushing this anthill of criminals with three kicks!'
'There's no need,' replied the philosopher. 'They'll destroy themselves on their own.
And besides, the real culprits are the leaders, who stay comfortably in their palaces.'
To change the subject, Micromégas asked a big question: 'What is the soul?'
The philosophers all answered at the same time, and each one had a different answer.
The first quoted Aristotle, the second Descartes, the third Leibniz.
Only a follower of Locke said: 'I don't know how I think, but I know that I only think thanks to my senses.'
It was the wisest answer, and Micromégas smiled.
But there was also on the ship a little man in a square hat: a theologian.
He looked at the two giants, and he said confidently: 'I know the truth.
The universe, the stars, the planets, and even you two: everything was created only for man.'
When they heard that, the two giants laughed so hard that they almost fell over.
The ship fell into the Saturnian's pocket, and they had trouble finding it again.
Before leaving, Micromégas wanted to be generous to these little beings.
'I'm going to give you a book,' he said. 'In this book, you will find the answer to all your questions, and you will see the meaning of all things.'
The philosophers took the book to Paris, to the Academy of Sciences.
The old secretary of the Academy opened it with emotion.

au: to the, at the, in the
coupé: cut (s'est coupé = cut off for himself)
dire: to say (il faut dire = it must be said)
doutais: suspected (je m'en doutais = I thought as much)
envie: desire (avoir envie de = to feel like)
esprit: mind, wit (avoir de l'esprit = to be witty)
par: by, on (par terre = on the ground)
peine: à peine = barely; ce n'est pas la peine = no need
plus: more; no longer (ne … plus); most (le plus)
question: question
